name: Echinostoma spp.

taxonomy.rank_note: Reference groups can include multiple species. Protozoan higher-rank systems differ; the lineage is provided without forcing every clade into a class rank.

morphology: Egg: approximately 80–135 × 55–80 µm across described echinostomes; yellow-brown with a subtle operculum and sometimes abopercular thickening.
Adults have a collar of spines; this genus-level card is not a universal species key.

transmission.detail: Snail development is followed by encystment in a second intermediate host; eating infected aquatic hosts introduces intestinal adults.

life_cycle.detail: Snail development is followed by encystment in a second intermediate host; eating infected aquatic hosts introduces intestinal adults.

hosts: Definitive: mammals or birds depending on species. Intermediate: snail first; snails, other mollusks, fish or amphibians may follow.
distribution: Asian foci including Thailand; host and species distributions differ.
clinical_significance: Intestinal inflammation, diarrhea and abdominal pain; heavier infections may contribute to anemia.
diagnostics: Wet mounts and concentration at 100–400×; adult or molecular identification improves species certainty.
differential_diagnosis: Large operculated eggs overlap Fasciola and Fasciolopsis; collar spines are an adult feature, not an egg feature.
review_status: Source-compiled educational content; not independently clinically validated

annotation_guidance: Record specimen, stage, stain, objective/total magnification, pixel calibration, source image and reviewer certainty.
Native crops of 200–650 pixels do not determine biological size. Retain µm-per-pixel calibration before resizing.
Split training, validation and test data by patient/specimen; keep related crops in the same split.
Keep damaged or ambiguous objects uncertain. Molecular confirmation of a mixed specimen does not assign every pictured object a species.
